Near-optimal and Efficient First-Order Algorithm for Multi-Task Learning with Shared Linear Representation

Shihong Ding Affiliation: State Key Lab of General AI, School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University, China    Fangyu Du Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Peking University, China    Cong Fang Affiliation: State Key Lab of General AI, School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University, China Affiliation: Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Peking University, China Correspondence to: fangcong@pku.edu.cn
Abstract

Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm in machine learning by leveraging shared structures across multiple related tasks. Despite its empirical success, the development of likelihood-based efficiently solvable algorithms—even for shared linear representations—remains largely underdeveloped, primarily due to the non-convex structure intrinsic to matrix factorization. This paper introduces a first-order algorithm that jointly learns a shared representation and task-specific parameters, with guaranteed efficiency. Notably, it converges in 𝒪~​(1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1) iterations and attains a near-optimal estimation error of 𝒪~​(d​k/(T​N))\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(dk/(TN)), improving over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of kk, where dd, kk, TT, NN denote input dimension, representation dimension, task count, and samples per task, respectively. Our results justify that likelihood-based first-order methods can efficiently solve the MTL problem.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Multi-task learning (MTL) has become a fundamental paradigm in machine learning (Argyriou et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2007; Maurer et al., 2012; Zhang, 2013; Zhao et al., 2025b), addressing a core challenge of real-world intelligence: the ability to learn multiple related tasks while leveraging their inherent commonalities. Unlike isolated single-task models, MTL frameworks are designed to exploit a shared structure that are learned using whole data across the tasks, thereby improving data efficiency. Related paradigms including transfer learning (TL) and meta-learning (Maurer et al., 2016; Finn et al., 2017; Snell et al., 2017; Aqeel et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) also build on leveraging shared structures that are then transferred to new tasks to improve generalization. Among various MTL and TL approaches, a central and widely adopted strategy is to assume that all tasks share a common or similar underlying representation, on which predictions for each task are based. This formulation transforms the problem into the joint learning of both a shared representation function and individual task-specific predictors. Gradient descent based algorithm applied to the corresponding log-likelihood objective is the most common approach for solving the problem. In neural network models, this is typically implemented through forward and backward propagation, a procedure central to modern deep learning practice. The effectiveness of shared representation learning has been empirically witnessed across diverse domains, including object detection (Zhang et al., 2014), language understanding evaluation (Wang et al., 2018), affective computing (Kollias et al., 2024), and drug design (Allenspach et al., 2024).

On the theoretical side, most studies focus on establishing statistical guarantees for multi-task representation learning. Pioneering works by Baxter (2000), Ando et al. (2005), and Maurer et al. (2016), for example, analyze general function classes and demonstrate that the statistical error for the shared function depends on samples from all tasks, thereby offering provable generalization improvements in various settings. Subsequent studies (Agarwal et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2022; Collins et al., 2024) examine more specific function classes—such as linear or neural network representations—and derive improved or near-optimal sample complexity bounds. Another line of research explores more complex frameworks, including models with similar rather than identical representations, multi-task reinforcement learning in Markov decision processes, and distributed learning settings.

In machine learning, we value not only statistical efficiency but also the availability of efficient and practical algorithms to solve a given problem. However, the solvability of multi-task representation learning—even for shared linear representations—remains largely open. This challenge stems from its underlying mathematical structure: the joint learning of a shared representation and task-specific predictors typically takes the form of a matrix factorization problem, which is inherently non-convex and often computationally difficult to solve globally. For linear representation learning, the first work to study the solvability through efficient algorithms is Tripuraneni et al. (2021). It examines the global convergence of first-order methods based on the likelihood function. However, this analysis relies on a technical assumption that the point of convergence is an interior point of a predetermined region. Although Thekumparampil et al. (2021) further proposes a likelihood-based method with a simpler update rule, the resulting estimation error bound 𝒪~​(d​k2N​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk^{2}}{NT}) remains sub-optimal, as the known information-theoretic lower bound for this setting is 𝒪~​(d​kN​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk}{NT}) (Tripuraneni et al., 2021; Tian et al., 2025), where dd, kk, TT, NN denote input dimension, representation dimension, task count, and samples per task, respectively. To ensure computational tractability and achieve optimal sample complexity, subsequent research has turned to methods of moments (Niu et al., 2024) or spectral approaches (Tian et al., 2025), avoiding the non-convex matrix factorization structure. However, these types of methods often rely heavily on problem-specific structures, such as noise assumption, and require careful algorithmic design.

In contrast,likelihood-based methods, which typically adopt maximum likelihood estimation as the training objective, possibly augmented with regularization, are among the most widely used approaches in machine learning practice. Within the problem, applying first-order algorithm over the factorization structure in order to jointly learn representations and predictors is ubiquitous in machine learning. However, it remains an open challenge to design a computationally efficient likelihood-based algorithm that attains statistical optimality, even for the linear representation setting.

This paper focuses on this canonical high-dimensional MTL with low-rank linear representations (Linear MTL) and designs the first first-order likelihood-based algorithm that jointly learns a shared representation and task-specific parameters, with guaranteed computational and statistical efficiency. Specifically, consider TT tasks and NN samples {(𝐱t(i),yt(i))}i∈[N]\{(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(i)},y_{t}^{(i)})\}_{i\in[N]} on each task t∈[T]t\in[T]. For task t∈[T]t\in[T], with 𝐱t(i)∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} being the covariate and yt(i)y_{t}^{(i)} being its response, we assume a linear relationship:

yt(i)=⟨𝐱t(i),𝐯t∗⟩+zt(i),y_{t}^{(i)}=\left\langle\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(i)},\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*}\right\rangle+z_{t}^{(i)},

where 𝐯t∗∈ℝd\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the task specific parameter and zt(i)∈ℝz_{t}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R} is an additive noise. We suppose a low-dimensional structure on the parameters, where there is an matrix 𝐁∗∈ℝd×k\mathbf{B}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} with k≤T≤dk\leq T\leq d and vectors 𝐰t∗∈ℝk\mathbf{w}_{t}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} such that 𝐯t∗=𝐁∗​𝐰t∗\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*}=\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{w}_{t}^{*} for all tt. Here 𝐁∗\mathbf{B}^{*} is the shared low-dimensional representation and 𝐰t∗\mathbf{w}_{t}^{*} is the task-specific parameter for task tt. The goal is to estimate (𝐯1∗,⋯,𝐯T∗)(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{*},\cdots,\mathbf{v}_{T}^{*}).

The main novelty of our algorithmic design is a two-phase gradient descent (TPGD) algorithm. The first phase (warm-start) performs unregularized gradient descent on the negative log-likelihood function

ℒ^​(𝐁,𝐖):=12​N​∑t=1T∑i=1N(yt(i)−⟨𝐱t(i),𝐁𝐰t⟩)2,\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{L}}\left(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W}\right):=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(y_{t}^{(i)}-\left\langle\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(i)},\mathbf{B}\mathbf{w}_{t}\right\rangle\right)^{2}, (1)

where 𝐖=(𝐰1,⋯,𝐰t)\mathbf{W}=(\mathbf{w}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{w}_{t}). This phase conducts feature learning and ensures that, starting from random initialization, the parameters 𝐁\mathbf{B} and 𝐖\mathbf{W} converge within a small neighborhood of the global optimum after 𝒪~​(1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1) iterations, overcoming the non-convex barrier of the objective function. The second phase (refined optimization with correction) performs regularized gradient descent to guarantee statical efficiency with the following update rules:

{𝐁(τ+1)=𝐁(τ)−η​∇𝐁ℒ^​(𝐁(τ),𝐖(τ))−η2​𝐁(τ)​[(𝐁(τ))⊤​𝐁(τ)−𝐖(τ)​(𝐖(τ))⊤],𝐖(τ+1)=𝐖(τ)−η​∇𝐖ℒ^​(𝐁(τ),𝐖(τ))−η2​[𝐖(τ)​(𝐖(τ))⊤−(𝐁(τ))⊤​𝐁(τ)]​𝐖(τ).\displaystyle\begin{cases}\mathbf{B}^{(\tau+1)}=\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}-\eta\nabla_{\mathbf{B}}\widehat{\mathcal{L}}\left(\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)},\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\right)\\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,-\frac{\eta}{2}\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}\left[\left(\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}\right)^{\top}\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}-\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\right)^{\top}\right],\\ \mathbf{W}^{(\tau+1)}=\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}-\eta\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}\widehat{\mathcal{L}}\left(\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)},\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\right)\\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,-\frac{\eta}{2}\left[\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\right)^{\top}-\left(\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}\right)^{\top}\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}\right]\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}.\end{cases} (2)

Consequently, the proposed algorithm has an iteration complexity of only 𝒪~​(1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1), and achieves a convergence rate of 𝒪~​(d​kN​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk}{NT}) for estimation error 1T​∑t=1T‖𝐯^t−𝐯t∗‖2\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}-\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*}\right\|^{2}. This rate matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors, improving over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of kk. See Table 1 for a comparison of different algorithms on linear MTL.

We would emphasize that achieving the 𝒪~​(1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1) iteration complexity and 𝒪~​(d​k)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(dk) sample complexity for this matrix factorization problem is technically nontrivial. A closely related setting is matrix sensing, where the goal is to recover a low-rank matrix from linear measurements. Under the factorization formulation, the best known first-order algorithms achieve iteration complexity of 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{k}) and sample complexity of 𝒪⁡(d​k2)\mathcal{O}(dk^{2}) for symmetric ground truth, and 𝒪⁡(d8)\mathcal{O}(d^{8}) and 𝒪⁡(d​k3)\mathcal{O}(dk^{3}) for the general case. It remains an open question whether statistical optimality can be attained via first-order methods. In contrast, linear MTL differs from matrix sensing notably in its noise structure. In this work, we attain the optimal estimation complexity within 𝒪~​(1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1) iterations. The key novelty in our theoretical analysis lies in our examination of the feature learning capability in Phase I and the rapid convergence property in Phase II.

Our Contributions. The contributions of this paper are as follows:

  1. (1)

    We propose a two-stage first-order likelihood-based algorithm for Linear MLT.

  2. (2)

    The algorithm is the first to achieve computational efficiency with a near-optimal estimation error of 𝒪~​(d​k/(T​N))\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(dk/(TN)), improving over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of kk.

2 Related Work

Multi-Task Learning and Transfer Learning. The goal of MTL is to improve the accuracy of individual task models through joint learning across multiple related tasks (Argyriou et al., 2008; Maurer et al., 2012; Zhang, 2013; Liu et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2010). And the goal of TL is to transfer knowledge from one task to another. For theoretical analysis of MTL and TL, Baxter (2000) studies a model under general function classes where tasks with shared representations are sampled from the same underlying environment, which was later improved in subsequent works (Pontil and Maurer, 2013; Maurer et al., 2016). Ando et al. (2005) proposes a framework to learn a shared low-dimensional predictive representation from multiple tasks. Under linear settings, Du et al. (2021); Duan and Wang (2023) provide the generalization ability of ERM for the likelihood function, and Thekumparampil et al. (2021) designs a polynomial-time alternating gradient descent algorithm that achieves similar performance as ERM but avoids solving the non-convex optimization directly. Tripuraneni et al. (2021); Duchi et al. (2022); Niu et al. (2024) propose the solvable moment methods. Tian et al. (2025) design spectral methods via SVD with task contamination. Other studies have extensively examined loss error bounds for complex MTL representation models, such as those based on Markov decision processes (Agarwal et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2022) and two-layer ReLU neural networks (Collins et al., 2024). (Jacob et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2011) study models with similar rather than identical representations, while (Smith et al., 2017; Marfoq et al., 2021; Corinzia et al., 2019) investigate MTL under distributed learning setting.

Matrix Sensing. It’s a classical problem aimed at recovering a low-rank matrix from measurement data. Due to its non-convex nature and its connection to key phenomena in deep learning theory (Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Arora et al., 2019; Soltanolkotabi et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2023), matrix sensing also serves as an important testbed for studying the convergence behavior of deep learning models. Specifically, Li et al. (2018); Li et al. (2020); Arora et al. (2019); Soltanolkotabi et al. (2023) demonstrate that gradient descent exhibits an implicit regularization effect when training over-parameterized matrix factorization models, enabling convergence to the underlying low-rank matrix that generated the measurements. Furthermore, Xiong et al. (2023) proves that an asymmetric parameterization can achieve exponential acceleration in convergence. At the population level, the likelihood functions of the matrix sensing problem and linear MTL are identical, indicating a structural correlation between them. There exists linear MTL study leverage this connection. For instance, building on Recht et al. (2010)’s technique for solving nuclear norm minimization problem, Zhang et al. (2024) develops a method that learns the task-invariant subspace to address data scarcity in linear MTL. However, the noise structures of matrix sensing problem and linear MTL differ fundamentally: the former arises from random measurement matrices, while the latter originates from random observation vectors per task. Consequently, linear MTL and matrix sensing exhibit an essential difference in their computational complexity and sample complexity. The algorithmic design and theoretical analysis in this work are inspired by literature in matrix sensing (Tu et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2023). However, our method exhibits substantial advantages in complexity, requiring only 𝒪~​(1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1) computational complexity and 𝒪~​(d​k)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(dk) sample complexity, compared to 𝒪~​(poly​(d))\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\text{poly}(d)) and 𝒪~​(d​k2)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(dk^{2}) for existing approaches, respectively.

3 Problem Formulation

Setup. This work investigate a setting with TT tasks and high-dimensional condition d>Td>T. Each task t∈[T]t\in[T] is associated with the data space 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, where 𝒳⊆ℝd\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the covariate space and 𝒴⊆ℝ\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R} denotes the response space. For each task t∈[T]t\in[T], we have access to NN samples: (𝐱t(1),yt(1)),⋯,(𝐱t(N),yt(N))(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(1)},y_{t}^{(1)}),\cdots,(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(N)},y_{t}^{(N)}). For notational convenience, we define the covariate data matrix 𝐗t:=(𝐱t(1),⋯,𝐱t(N))\mathbf{X}_{t}:=(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(1)},\cdots,\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(N)}) and response data vector 𝐲t:=(yt(1),⋯,yt(N))\mathbf{y}_{t}:=(y_{t}^{(1)},\cdots,y_{t}^{(N)}) for each task tt. In this work, the common feature is characterized by a linear representation function ϕ:𝒳→𝒵⊆ℝk\phi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{k}, where k<min⁡{d,T}k<\min\{d,T\}. Specifically, for each task t∈[T]t\in[T], we define the predictive function as 𝐱→⟨ϕ⁡(𝐱),𝐰t⟩:=⟨𝐱t,𝐁𝐰t⟩\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\langle\phi(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{w}_{t}\rangle:=\langle\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{B}\mathbf{w}_{t}\rangle, where 𝐁∈ℝd×k\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} and 𝐰t∈ℝk\mathbf{w}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}. Let 𝐖\mathbf{W} denote the matrix formed by aggregating all task-specific weight vectors, i.e., 𝐖=(𝐰1,…,𝐰T)∈ℝk×T\mathbf{W}=\left(\mathbf{w}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{w}_{T}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times T}. Using training samples from the TT tasks, the representation and task-specific parameters can be learned by solving the following optimization problem:

min𝐁∈ℝd×k𝐖∈ℝk×T{ℒ^(𝐁,𝐖)=12​N∑t=1T‖𝐲t−𝐗t⊤𝐁𝐰t‖2}.\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\atop\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times T}}\left\{\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\mathbf{y}_{t}-\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{w}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right\}. (3)

Let 𝐁^\widehat{\mathbf{B}} and 𝐖^\widehat{\mathbf{W}} denote the representation and task-specific matrix obtained by numerically solving the optimization problem in Eq. (3). We first address whether the predictor 𝐁^​𝐖^\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\widehat{\mathbf{W}} achieves a strong recover of the ground-truth 𝐁∗​𝐖∗:=(𝐯1∗,⋯,𝐯T∗)\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{W}^{*}:=(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{*},\cdots,\mathbf{v}_{T}^{*}). Then we apply the learned representation 𝐁^\widehat{\mathbf{B}} to a target task T+1T+1. Suppose the target task is defined by a distribution ρ\rho over 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, from which we draw MM i.i.d. samples: (𝐱T+1(1),yT+1(1)),⋯,(𝐱T+1(M),yT+1(M))(\mathbf{x}_{T+1}^{(1)},y_{T+1}^{(1)}),\cdots,(\mathbf{x}_{T+1}^{(M)},y_{T+1}^{(M)}). Using ϕ^\widehat{\phi}, we train a linear predictor by solving the following optimization problem:

min𝐰T+1∈ℝk⁡Lρ​(𝐁^,𝐰T+1),\min_{\mathbf{w}_{T+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}}L_{\rho}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},{\mathbf{w}}_{T+1}),

where Lρ(𝐁^,𝐰T+1):=12𝔼(𝐱T+1,yT+1)∼ρ[(yT+1−⟨𝐱T+1,L_{\rho}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},{\mathbf{w}}_{T+1}):=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}_{T+1},y_{T+1})\sim\rho}[(y_{T+1}-\langle\mathbf{x}_{T+1}, 𝐁^𝐰T+1⟩)2]\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\mathbf{w}_{T+1}\rangle)^{2}]. Let 𝐰^T+1\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{T+1} denote the numerical solution to this problem. We analyze the generalization performance of the predictor 𝐁^​𝐰^T+1\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{T+1} to the target task. Specifically, we aim to ensure that the population loss Lρ​(𝐁^,𝐰^T+1)L_{\rho}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{T+1}) is sufficiently small.

Data Assumption. We assume the existence of a ground-truth representation 𝐁∗∈ℝd×k\mathbf{B}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} and task-specific parameters 𝐰1∗,⋯,𝐰T∗,𝐰T+1∗∈ℝk\mathbf{w}_{1}^{*},\cdots,\mathbf{w}_{T}^{*},\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, such that for every task t∈[T+1]t\in[T+1], the equality 𝔼⁡[yt|𝐱t]=⟨𝐱t,𝐁∗​𝐰t∗⟩\mathbb{E}[y_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{t}]=\left\langle\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{w}_{t}^{*}\right\rangle holds. More specifically, we assume that for each task t∈[T+1]t\in[T+1], the response yty_{t} given the covariate 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is generated as follows:

yt=⟨𝐱t,𝐁∗​𝐰t∗⟩+zt,zt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2),\displaystyle y_{t}=\left\langle\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{w}_{t}^{*}\right\rangle+z_{t},\qquad z_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), (4)

where 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and ztz_{t} are independent for all t∈[T+1]t\in[T+1]. For the covariate data matrices {𝐗t}t=1T\{\mathbf{X}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, we require them to satisfy the restricted isometry property (RIP). Before introducing specific assumptions, we first present the definition of RIP.

Definition 3.1 (Restricted Isometry Property (RIP)).

We say that a matrix 𝐗/N∈ℝd×N\mathbf{X}/\sqrt{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} satisfies the δ\delta-RIP if for every vector 𝐯∈ℝd\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the following inequality holds:

(1−δ)​‖𝐯‖2≤‖𝐗⊤​𝐯N‖2≤(1+δ)​‖𝐯‖2.(1-\delta)\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}\leq\left\|\frac{\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{v}}{\sqrt{N}}\right\|^{2}\leq(1+\delta)\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}.

During the learning process for the representation function, we state the following assumption:

Assumption 3.2.

There exists a constant δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) such that 𝐗t/N∈ℝd×N\mathbf{X}_{t}/\sqrt{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} satisfies the δ−\delta-RIP for any t∈[T]t\in[T].

The RIP is widely used in matrix sensing (Li et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2023) and over-parameterized regression (Vaskevicius et al., 2019; Woodworth et al., 2020). The setting considered in Tripuraneni et al. (2021), where the covariate data {𝐱i}\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\} is i.i.d. and sub-Gaussian, is in fact a special case of Assumption 3.2. Based on Candès and Plan (2011), if each entry of 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} follows an i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1/N)\mathcal{N}(0,1/N) distribution for all t∈[T]t\in[T], then 𝐗t/N\mathbf{X}_{t}/\sqrt{N} satisfies the δ\delta-RIP condition when N=Ω~​(d/δ2)N=\widetilde{\Omega}(d/\delta^{2}).

Below, we provide assumptions for task T+1T+1.

Assumption 3.3.

Denote 𝐇:=𝔼⁡[𝐱T+1​𝐱T+1⊤]\mathbf{H}:=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{x}_{T+1}\mathbf{x}_{T+1}^{\top}\right], and assume that 𝐇\mathbf{H} is strictly positive definite.

There exists a constant α>0\alpha>0, such that for every positive semi-definite (PSD) matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M}, the following inequality holds:

𝔼⁡[𝐱T+1​𝐱T+1⊤​𝐌𝐱T+1​𝐱T+1⊤]⪯α⁡⟨𝐇,𝐌⟩⋅𝐇.\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{x}_{T+1}\mathbf{x}_{T+1}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}_{T+1}\mathbf{x}_{T+1}^{\top}\right]\preceq\alpha\left\langle\mathbf{H},\mathbf{M}\right\rangle\cdot\mathbf{H}.

Assumption 3.3 is satisfied if 𝐇−1/2𝐱T+1∼𝒩(𝟎,𝐈𝐝)\mathbf{H}^{-1/2}\mathbf{x}_{T+1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bf{0},\mathbf{I}_{d}), in which case α=3\alpha=3. More generally, the assumption also holds for any covariate data 𝐱T+1\mathbf{x}_{T+1} whose kurtosis is bounded along every direction (Dieuleveut et al., 2017). It is a relatively weak moment condition and has been commonly used in analyses of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) (Dieuleveut et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2025a). Existing theoretical guarantees for TL (Tripuraneni et al., 2021; Du et al., 2021; Niu et al., 2024) typically require the covariate 𝐱T+1\mathbf{x}_{T+1} to be sub-Gaussian. In this work, we relax the assumption to a weaker moment condition specified in Assumption 3.3.

Estimation Error. For MTL, our focus is the estimation error 1T​∑t=1T‖𝐯^t−𝐯t‖2\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}-\mathbf{v}_{t}\right\|^{2}, same to Tian et al. (2025). Under the RIP condition (Candes and Tao, 2005; Recht et al., 2010) and mild moment assumption, this error bound also corresponds to the population loss 𝔼{(𝐗t,𝐲t)}t∈[T]​[1T​ℒ^​(𝐁^,𝐖^)]\mathbb{E}_{\{(\mathbf{X}_{t},\mathbf{y}_{t})\}_{t\in[T]}}[\frac{1}{T}\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},\widehat{\mathbf{W}})]. For TL, we focus on the excess risk Lρ​(𝐁^,𝐰T+1)L_{\rho}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},{\mathbf{w}}_{T+1}), same to (Du et al., 2021; Tripuraneni et al., 2021).

For clarity, we restate some key symbols: d,k,T,Nd,k,T,N denote the input dimension, representation dimension, task count, MTL per task sample size, respectively. κ,α~,δ~,K1,K2,M\kappa,\widetilde{\alpha},\widetilde{\delta},K_{1},K_{2},M represent the condition number κ⁡(𝚺∗)\kappa(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}), initial scaling, event probability, MTL iteration count, TL iteration count, TL sample size.

In our complexity analysis, following (Du et al., 2021; Tripuraneni et al., 2021; Niu et al., 2024), we treat κ⁡(𝚺∗)\kappa(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}) and α\alpha in Assumption 3.3 as constants in Corollaries 5.3 and 5.6, and focus exclusively on the dependence of the estimation error on d,k,T,N,K2d,k,T,N,K_{2}.

4 Algorithm

To recover the underlying representation 𝐁∗\mathbf{B}^{*} and task-specific matrix 𝐖∗\mathbf{W}^{*}, we propose a TPGD algorithm (Algorithm 1). Its iteration can be divided into two phase.

Phase I (Warm-Start): In this phase, the algorithm first performs K1K_{1} iterations of gradient descent on the function ℒ^​(𝐁,𝐖)\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W}) to obtain initial estimates 𝐁(K1/2)\mathbf{B}^{(K_{1}/2)} and 𝐖(K1/2)\mathbf{W}^{(K_{1}/2)}. Our analysis shows that this phase yields a coarse estimate that lies within a constant radius CC of the global optimum with high probability, serving as a qualified initialization for the second phase.

Phase II (Refined Optimization with Correction): In the second phase, we augment the update rules with correction terms

ℐ𝐁(τ):=\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}}:= 𝐁(τ)​[(𝐁(τ))⊤​𝐁(τ)−𝐖(τ)​(𝐖(τ))⊤],\displaystyle\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}\left[\left(\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}\right)^{\top}\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}-\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\right)^{\top}\right],
ℐ𝐖(τ):=\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}}:= [𝐖(τ)​(𝐖(τ))⊤−(𝐁(τ))⊤​𝐁(τ)]​𝐖(τ).\displaystyle\left[\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}\right)^{\top}-\left(\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}\right)^{\top}\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}\right]\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)}.

which are computed from the first-phase outputs (𝐁(K1/2),𝐖(K1/2))(\mathbf{B}^{(K_{1}/2)},\mathbf{W}^{(K_{1}/2)}). This is equivalent to performing gradient descent on a regularized objective,

ℒ~​(𝐁,𝐖)=ℒ^​(𝐁,𝐖)+18​‖𝐁⊤​𝐁−𝐖𝐖⊤‖F2.\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W})=\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W})+\frac{1}{8}\left\|\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}. (5)

The correction terms ℐ𝐁\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{B}} and ℐ𝐖\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{W}} are derived from the gradient of this regularization term. Their primary role is to mitigate the mutual coupling and interference between 𝐁\mathbf{B} and 𝐖\mathbf{W} during joint optimization——a challenge also prevalent in matrix sensing problems (Xiong et al., 2023). As detailed in Section 5, this modification leads to a faster convergence rate in optimization and, more importantly, yields a tighter generalization error bound.

5 Theoretical Analysis

In this section, we analyze the convergence of Algorithm 1 for the population loss of MTL (Section 5.1), and the generalization performance of the representation predictor learned by Algorithm 1 in the target task (Section 5.2).

5.1 Multi-Task Learning

Consider the singular value decomposition (SVD) of 𝐁∗​𝐖∗\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{W}^{*}, given by

𝐁∗​𝐖∗=𝐔∗​𝚺∗​𝐕∗⊤,\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{W}^{*}=\mathbf{U}^{*}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}{\mathbf{V}^{*}}^{\top},

where 𝐔∗∈ℝd×d\mathbf{U}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and 𝐕∗∈ℝT×T\mathbf{V}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T} are orthogonal matrices. The following theorem provides the convergence guarantee for Algorithm 1 when learning the representation function.

Theorem 5.1.

Under Assumption 3.2, suppose δ≲min\delta\lesssim\min {k−1/2κ−7/2,κ−6}\{k^{-1/2}\kappa^{-7/2},\kappa^{-6}\} and select the hyper-parameters as follows:

Then the output 𝐁^=𝐁(K1),𝐖^=𝐖(K1)\widehat{\mathbf{B}}=\mathbf{B}^{(K_{1})},\widehat{\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{W}^{(K_{1})} from the last iteration of Algorithm 1 satisfies

[dist((𝐁^𝐖^⊤),(𝐅𝐆))]2\displaystyle\left[\dist\left(\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\\ \widehat{\mathbf{W}}^{\top}\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{F}\\ \mathbf{G}\end{pmatrix}\right)\right]^{2}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim (1−σk​(𝚺∗)4​η2)K1/2​σk​(𝚺∗)+σ2⋅tr(𝚺∗)dσk2​(𝚺∗)​N,\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{\sigma_{k}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*})}{4}\eta_{2}\right)^{K_{1}/2}\sigma_{k}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*})+{\sigma^{2}}\cdot\frac{\tr\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}\right)d}{\sigma_{k}^{2}\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}\right)N},

with probability at least 1−δ~−C2​exp⁡(−C3​k)1-\widetilde{\delta}-C_{2}\exp(-C_{3}k) where C2,C3>0C_{2},C_{3}>0 denote fixed numerical constants, and

𝐅=\displaystyle\mathbf{F}= 𝐔∗​(⋅,[k])​(𝚺[k]∗)1/2∈ℝd×k,\displaystyle\mathbf{U}^{*}(\cdot,[k])(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{[k]}^{*})^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k},
𝐆=\displaystyle\mathbf{G}= 𝐕∗​(⋅,[k])​(𝚺[k]∗)1/2∈ℝT×k.\displaystyle\mathbf{V}^{*}(\cdot,[k])(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{[k]}^{*})^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times k}.
Remark 5.2.

One can notice that 𝐁∗\mathbf{B}^{*} and 𝐅\mathbf{F} are equivalent up to an invertible transformation 𝐏∈ℝk×k\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}, i.e., 𝐁∗=𝐅𝐏\mathbf{B}^{*}=\mathbf{F}\mathbf{P}. Consequently, treating κ⁡(𝚺∗)\kappa(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}) as a constant, Theorem 5.1 implies that [dist(𝐁^,𝐁∗​𝐏−1)]2≤𝒪~​(σ2​d​kσk​(𝚺∗)​N)[\dist(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{P}^{-1})]^{2}\leq\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{\sigma^{2}dk}{\sigma_{k}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*})N}). For the detailed derivation, we refer the reader to Section A.1 in the appendix. It is worth noting that directly applying the analysis of Xiong et al. (2023) to traditional gradient descent for linear low-rank MTL suffers two major challenges. (1) High computational complexity: Existing techniques guarantee convergence only when the step size is smaller than (poly​(d))−1(\text{poly}(d))^{-1}, requiring more than 𝒪~​(poly​(d))\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\text{poly}(d)) iterations. In contrast, Algorithm 1 allows a constant step size, achieving convergence within 𝒪~​(1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1) iterations. (2) Overly stringent RIP condition: Existing techniques require the RIP constant δ≲k−1\delta\lesssim k^{-1} for global convergence, which means that a sample size of N≳d​k2N\gtrsim dk^{2} per task is necessary under the Gaussian setting. Our algorithm only requires δ≲k−1/2\delta\lesssim k^{-1/2} in its first phase to converge to a neighborhood of the ground-truth, and further relaxes this to δ≲1\delta\lesssim 1 in the second phase. Thus, under the Gaussian setting, sample size N≳d​kN\gtrsim dk assumed in Theorem 5.1 is sufficient to ensure δ≲k−1/2\delta\lesssim k^{-1/2}.

The proof of Theorem 5.1 consists of two phases: Phase I and Phase II. The analysis for Phase I is inspired by the works of Soltanolkotabi et al. (2023) and Xiong et al. (2023). However, unlike their approaches, which focuses on approximating 𝐁∗​𝐖∗\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{W}^{*} by 𝐁𝐖\mathbf{B}\mathbf{W}, we prove that (𝐁,𝐖⊤)(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W}^{\top}) converges to a neighborhood of (𝐅,𝐆)(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{G}). This demonstrates that, starting from random initialization, Algorithm 1 learns the feature spaces of 𝐅\mathbf{F} and 𝐆\mathbf{G} already within Phase I, thereby establishing the feature-learning capability of this phase.

In Phase II, we prove the global convergence of the algorithm. Instead of adopting conventional convergence analyses from optimization theory—which typically construct a suitable convex (or strongly convex) energy function and relate the algorithm’s iterative trajectory to the convexity of this function—we decompose the distance error considered in Theorem 5.1 into two components: Part I, which is driven by the gradient of ℒ~\widetilde{\mathcal{L}} in Eq. (5) without additive noise, and Part II, which is generated by the additive noise. Part I is shown to exhibit linear convergence. Specifically, we show that the function ℒ~\widetilde{\mathcal{L}} without additive noise satisfies a Regularity Condition (Candes et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2016), which can be viewed as a form of strong convexity applicable to functions possessing rotational degrees of freedom at optimal points. Part II contributes an error term through cumulative summation, given by σ2tr(𝚺∗)dσk2​(𝚺∗)​N\frac{\sigma^{2}\tr\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}\right)d}{\sigma_{k}^{2}\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}\right)N}. This extension is necessary because, in the problem considered, rotational degrees of freedom prevent the construction of an energy function that is convex (or strongly convex) in any neighborhood of (𝐁∗,𝐖∗)(\mathbf{B}^{*},\mathbf{W}^{*}), except in the special case k=1k=1.

The following corollary implies that under the conditions T>kT>k and NN samples per task, the estimation error of MTL is strictly lower than that of learning TT task parameters independently (𝒪~​(d​kN​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk}{NT}) v.s. 𝒪~​(dN)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{d}{N})).

Corollary 5.3.

Suppose that the assumptions and hyper-parameter settings of Theorem 5.1 hold. Then, the MTL population loss achieved by Algorithm 1 satisfies

1T​∑t=1T‖𝐯^t−𝐯t∗‖2≲σ2⋅d​kN​T,\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}-\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*}\right\|^{2}\lesssim\sigma^{2}\cdot\frac{dk}{NT},

where 𝐯t∗:=𝐁∗​𝐰t∗\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*}:=\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{w}_{t}^{*} and 𝐯^t:=𝐁^​𝐰^t\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}:=\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{t} for any t∈[T]t\in[T].

The best known likelihood-based method (Tripuraneni et al., 2021; Du et al., 2021; Thekumparampil et al., 2021; Duan and Wang, 2023; Tian et al., 2025) achieve a convergence rate of 𝒪~​(d​k2N​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk^{2}}{NT}) for the population loss 1T​∑t=1T‖𝐯^t−𝐯t∗‖2\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}-\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*}\|^{2}. According to Corollary 5.3, our algorithm attains a faster rate of 𝒪~​(d​kN​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk}{NT}). This rate matches the known lower bound (Tripuraneni et al., 2021; Tian et al., 2025) up to logarithmic factors. While Corollary 5.3 is primarily established under the high-dimensional regime where d>Td>T, it provides a general population loss bound of 𝒪~​(max⁡{d,T}​kN​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{\max\{d,T\}k}{NT}). Therefore, in the regime where T≥dT\geq d, Algorithm 1 also achieves a superior loss bound of 𝒪~​(kN)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{k}{N}), outperforming the 𝒪~​(dN)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{d}{N}) bound associated with learning TT task parameters independently.

5.2 Transfer Learning

We consider the T+1T+1 task is trained by SGD with decay step size, which is shown in Algorithm 2 in Appendix A.2.

Theorem 5.4.

Under Assumption 3.2 and Assumption 3.3, suppose δ≲min{k−1/2κ−7/2,κ−6}\delta\lesssim\min\{k^{-1/2}\kappa^{-7/2},\kappa^{-6}\} and select the hyper-parameters Eq. (6) and

η0≲1αtr(𝐁^⊤𝐇𝐁^),K2≳max{ασ2​η0,12​η0​σk​(𝐁^⊤​𝐇​𝐁^)}.\displaystyle\eta_{0}\lesssim\frac{1}{\alpha\tr\left(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\right)},K_{2}\gtrsim\max\left\{\frac{\alpha}{\sigma^{2}\eta_{0}},\frac{1}{2\eta_{0}\sigma_{k}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\right)}\right\}.

Then the output 𝐰T+1(K2)\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{(K_{2})} from the last iteration of stochastic gradient descent (Algorithm 2 in Appendix) satisfies

Lρ​(𝐁^,𝐰T+1(K2))−Lρ​(𝐁∗,𝐰T+1∗)\displaystyle L_{\rho}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{(K_{2})})-L_{\rho}(\mathbf{B}^{*},\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{*})
≲\displaystyle\lesssim σ2​‖𝐰T+1∗‖2​[(1+β12)​‖𝐇‖op+1+β22]⋅tr(𝚺∗)dσk2​(𝚺∗)​N\displaystyle\sigma^{2}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{*}\right\|^{2}\left[\left(1+\beta_{1}^{2}\right)\left\|\mathbf{H}\right\|_{\op}+1+\beta_{2}^{2}\right]\cdot\frac{\tr\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*}\right)d}{\sigma_{k}^{2}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*})N}

where β1:=‖(𝐇1/2​𝐁∗)†‖op\beta_{1}:=\|\left(\mathbf{H}^{1/2}\mathbf{B}^{*}\right)^{\dagger}\|_{\op} and β2:=‖𝐁∗‖op​‖𝐇‖op\beta_{2}:=\|\mathbf{B}^{*}\|_{\op}\|\mathbf{H}\|_{\op}.

Remark 5.5.

Under the constraint of a maximum sample size MM in TL phase, the online nature of Algorithm 2 implies that M=K2M=K_{2}. Given orthogonal matrix 𝐔~∈ℝd×k\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}, suppose 𝐔~⊤​𝐱T+1\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{T+1} satisfies the RIP with δ≲1\delta\lesssim 1. Then applying the ERM methods of Du et al. (2021); Tripuraneni et al. (2021) for linear regression on the target task T+1T+1 yields a convergence rate analogous to that in Theorem 5.4, under the condition that the transfer sample size M≳kM\gtrsim k. In contrast, Theorem 5.4 is established under a much weaker assumption, requiring only that covariate 𝐱T+1\mathbf{x}_{T+1} satisfies mild moment conditions.

In this section, we optimize 𝐰T+1\mathbf{w}_{T+1} while fixing the representation 𝐁^\widehat{\mathbf{B}} fixed. Compared with the typical dynamics of SGD with decaying step size in linear models (Wu et al., 2022), the variance component of SGD in this TL setting contains an additional term arising from both additive noise and the irreducible approximation error dist(𝐁^,𝐁∗)\dist(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},\mathbf{B}^{*}). This error further introduces stochastic noise that is correlated with the covariate 𝐱T+1\mathbf{x}_{T+1}. To address the statistical dependence caused by this correlation, we employ a block-wise variance decomposition technique, which provides a fine-grained analysis of the variance error, along with a recursive analysis that yields an iteration-wise estimate of the variance.

Corollary 5.6.

Suppose that the assumptions and hyper-parameter settings of Theorem 5.4 hold, and assume ‖𝐯t∗‖=𝒪⁡(1)\|\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*}\|=\mathcal{O}(1). Then the output 𝐰T+1(K2)\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{(K_{2})} from the last iteration of stochastic gradient descent (Algorithm 2 in Appendix) satisfies

Lρ​(𝐁^,𝐰T+1(K2))−Lρ​(𝐁∗,𝐰T+1∗)\displaystyle L_{\rho}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}},\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{(K_{2})})-L_{\rho}(\mathbf{B}^{*},\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{*})
≲\displaystyle\lesssim σ2​[(1+β12)​‖𝐇‖op+1+β22]⋅d​k2N​T+σ2​kK2,\displaystyle\sigma^{2}\left[\left(1+\beta_{1}^{2}\right)\left\|\mathbf{H}\right\|_{\op}+1+\beta_{2}^{2}\right]\cdot\frac{dk^{2}}{NT}+\frac{\sigma^{2}k}{K_{2}}, (8)

where β1:=‖(𝐇1/2​𝐁∗)†‖op\beta_{1}:=\|\left(\mathbf{H}^{1/2}\mathbf{B}^{*}\right)^{\dagger}\|_{\op} and β2:=‖𝐁∗‖op​‖𝐇‖op\beta_{2}:=\|\mathbf{B}^{*}\|_{\op}\|\mathbf{H}\|_{\op}.

The convergence rate of our algorithm in Eq. (8) matches the best known rate 𝒪~​(d​k2N​T+kM)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk^{2}}{NT}+\frac{k}{M}) up to logarithmic factors for likelihood-based low-dimensional linear representation TL methods. Under the additional assumption 𝔼⁡[‖𝐰T+1‖2]≲1/k\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{w}_{T+1}\|^{2}]\lesssim 1/k introduced by Du et al. (2021) (Theorem 4.1), the convergence rate of our algorithm achieves 𝒪~​(d​kN​T+kM)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk}{NT}+\frac{k}{M}).

6 Numerical Simulations

This section provides numerical simulations of TPGD, focusing on its convergence rate advantage with respect to both the total number of iterations and the sample size.

We compare the estimation error curves of Algorithm 1 against three comparative LBM algorithms for MTL, which have tractable update rule and require no per-iteration matrix decomposition (e.g., SVD or QR). The comparison also includes the theoretical estimation error curve derived in Section 5. All algorithms are applied to the same MTL problem defined in Section 3. The experiments consist of two groups, presented from top to bottom, under fixed input dimension dd, representation dimension kk, and task count TT. The first group (Figure 1) examines the convergence rate with respect to the total number of iterations for fixed per-task sample sizes. The second group (Figure 2) evaluates the convergence rate with respect to the per-task sample size for fixed total numbers of iterations. The theoretical curve is given by 𝒪~​(d​kN​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{dk}{NT}). Hence, when per-task sample size NN is fixed, this curve appears as a horizontal line.

In the experiments, the curve labeled “TPGD” represents the last-iterate estimation error of Algorithm 1. The “GD + Loss 1” curve corresponds to the tail-averaging estimation error of constant-step-size gradient descent (GD) applied to the Phase I loss (Eq. (3)). The “GD + Loss 2” curve denotes the tail-averaging estimation error of a constant-step-size GD method applied to the loss function from Tripuraneni et al. (2021), which is defined as

12​N​∑t=1T‖𝐲t−𝐗t⊤​𝐁𝐰t‖2+12​‖𝐁⊤​𝐁−𝐖𝐖⊤‖F2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\mathbf{y}_{t}-\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{w}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}. (9)

The “NSGD” curve represents the tail-averaging estimation error of the Noise-Scheduled SGD method (Fang et al., 2019) on the loss given in Eq. (9).

All comparative algorithms are initialized in the same manner as Algorithm 1, employing the recommended or default hyper-parameters from their original publications. The hyper-parameters for Algorithm 1 are set following the guidelines of Theorem 5.1, with the theoretical values scaled by a constant factor. Specifically, the Phase I step size η1\eta_{1} is scaled by a constant factor 1.1, while the Phase II step size η2\eta_{2} is taken as 0.1 times the theoretical value. For “GD + Loss 1”, which lacks specific recommendations, we set its step size to match the Phase I step size of TPGD.

As shown in Figure 1, Algorithm 1 exhibits the fastest convergence in reducing the estimation error when the per-task sample size NN is fixed. Figure 2 further demonstrates that Algorithm 1 also achieves the lowest estimation error among all algorithms compared. In summary, these results indicate that our algorithm holds a notable efficiency advantage over existing tractable LBM algorithms for MTL, which have no per-iteration steps (e.g., SVD or QR).

7 Conclusion

This work provides an efficiently likelihood-based first-order algorithm for MTL with a shared linear representation. Our results justify that principled likelihood optimization, despite its inherent non-convexity, can be achieved with both computational efficiency and statistical near-optimality in the MTL setting.

In Appendix A.3, we extend the analysis to the regime where task noise variances are heterogeneous. There, we study a curriculum learning strategy wherein tasks are first grouped and then learned sequentially in order of increasing noise variance. We provide a theoretical justification for the advantage of this incremental scheme over training all tasks at the same time.

A.1 Proof of Theorem 5.1

The analysis in Phase I is inspired by the works of (Soltanolkotabi et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2023). However, while their focus lies on approximating 𝐁∗​𝐖∗\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{W}^{*} by 𝐁𝐖\mathbf{B}\mathbf{W}, we instead prove that (𝐁,𝐖⊤)\left(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W}^{\top}\right) converges to a neighborhood of (𝐅,𝐆)\left(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{G}\right), where 𝐅=𝐔∗​(⋅,[k])​(𝚺[k]∗)1/2∈ℝd×k\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{U}^{*}(\cdot,[k])(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{[k]}^{*})^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} and 𝐆=𝐕∗​(⋅,[k])​(𝚺[k]∗)1/2∈ℝT×k\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{V}^{*}(\cdot,[k])(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{[k]}^{*})^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times k}. Specifically, we establish

dist((𝐁𝐖⊤),(𝐅𝐆))≤σk1/2​(𝚺∗)8.\dist\left(\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{B}\\ \mathbf{W}^{\top}\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{F}\\ \mathbf{G}\end{pmatrix}\right)\leq\frac{\sigma_{k}^{1/2}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{*})}{8}.

Our proof primarily analyzes the dynamics of the projected parameter matrices 𝐁~\widetilde{\mathbf{B}} and 𝐖~⊤\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}^{\top} (defined in Eq. (10) and Eq. (11)), which lie in the subspace spanned by 𝐔∗\mathbf{U}^{*} and 𝐕∗\mathbf{V}^{*}. The stochastic error induced by label noise zz is bounded via Lemma B.1. A further block-wise analysis of the iterative updates for 𝐁~\widetilde{\mathbf{B}} and 𝐖~\widetilde{\mathbf{W}} reveals that the following quantities remain consistently small throughout this phase:

  1. ∙\bullet

    ‖𝐁~[k],[k]−𝐖~[k],[k]⊤‖\left\|\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{[k],[k]}-\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{[k],[k]}^{\top}\right\|, the operator norm of the difference between the top k×kk\times k submatrices of 𝐁~\widetilde{\mathbf{B}} and 𝐖~⊤\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}^{\top}.

  2. ∙\bullet

    ‖𝐁~[k+1:d],[k]‖\left\|\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{[k+1:d],[k]}\right\| and ‖𝐖~[k],[k+1:T]⊤‖\left\|\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{[k],[k+1:T]}^{\top}\right\|, the operator norms of the corresponding trailing submatrices of 𝐁~\widetilde{\mathbf{B}} and 𝐖~⊤\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}^{\top}.

Combining these error estimates with Lemma B.2 completes the proof for Phase I.

Phase II of Algorithm 2 employs gradient descent with a regularization term. Here, we aim to prove that the distance between (𝐁,𝐖⊤)\left(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W}^{\top}\right) and (𝐅,𝐆)\left(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{G}\right) converges throughout the algorithm’s updates. In conventional convergence analyses of optimization algorithms, one often constructs a suitable convex (or strongly convex) energy function and relates the iterative trajectory of the algorithm to the convexity of this function to establish convergence. However, in the problem we consider, any optimal point possesses rotational degrees of freedom, which prevents the construction of such a convex (or strongly convex) energy function. Therefore, we adopt an approach based on designing an appropriate loss function and verifying that it satisfies the Regularity Condition which is introduced in prior works (Tu et al., 2016; Candes et al., 2015). This condition provides a sufficient criterion for convergence and relies only on first-order information along specific trajectories.

We have shown that the output (𝐁(K1/2),(𝐖K1/2)⊤)\left(\mathbf{B}^{(K_{1}/2)},(\mathbf{W}^{K_{1}/2})^{\top}\right) from Phase I lies within a neighborhood of (𝐅,𝐆)\left(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{G}\right). In Phase II, we prove that the noise error arising from the covariate vectors {𝐱t(i)}i=1N\{\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} in each task tt can be bounded to an appropriate magnitude. This enables us to further establish that the component of the loss gradient formed by these covariate vectors satisfies a certain Regularity Condition. Under this condition, the distance between (𝐁(τ),(𝐖(τ))⊤)\left(\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)},(\mathbf{W}^{(\tau)})^{\top}\right) and (𝐅,𝐆)\left(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{G}\right) decays linearly for τ∈[K1/2:K1]\tau\in[K_{1}/2:K_{1}] when label noise is disregarded. Consequently, we demonstrate that this distance comprises two distinct components: a deterministic error term that decreases linearly, and a stochastic error term induced by label noise, the latter of which can be controlled by the sample size NN.

A.1.2 Preliminary

Before proceeding to the proof of Phase II, we first introduce some preliminary knowledge. For a general function f:ℝd→ℝ+f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}, ensuring that a numerical method can find its global minimum typically requires ff to be convex or strongly convex. For a loss function on matrix F:ℝd×k→ℝ+F:\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}, there often exists rotational invariance around its global optima. Consequently, unless in the special case k=1k=1, FF is generally neither convex nor strongly convex in any neighborhood of a global optimum. To handle loss functions with such rotational freedom, Candes et al. (2015) and Tu et al. (2016) introduce a regularity condition (RC)—a property analogous to strong convexity—and showed that it is satisfied for problems such as quadratic equations solving, matrix factorization, and offline matrix sensing. Next, we formally define the RC as follows:

Definition A.2 (Regularity Condition).

Let 𝐉∈ℝd×k\mathbf{J}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} be a global optimum of F⁡(⋅)F(\cdot). Define the neighborhood B⁡(δ^)B(\hat{\delta}) as

B⁡(δ^):={𝐙∈ℝd×k:dist(𝐙,𝐉)≤δ^}.B(\hat{\delta}):=\left\{\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}:\dist(\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{J})\leq\hat{\delta}\right\}.

We say F⁡(⋅)F(\cdot) satisfies the regularity condition RC⁡(α,β,δ^)\mathrm{RC}(\alpha,\beta,\hat{\delta}) if for all matrices 𝐙∈B⁡(δ^)\mathbf{Z}\in B(\hat{\delta}) the following inequality holds

⟨∇F​(𝐙),𝐙−𝐉𝐑⟩≥1α​‖𝐙−𝐉𝐑‖F2+1β​‖∇F​(𝐙)‖F2,\left\langle\nabla F(\mathbf{Z}),\mathbf{Z}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{R}\right\rangle\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\left\|\mathbf{Z}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{R}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\frac{1}{\beta}\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{Z})\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2},

for some orthogonal matrix 𝐑∈ℝk×k\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}.

Specifically, Tu et al. (2016) define a reference function L⁡(𝐙):=14​‖𝐙𝐙⊤−𝐉𝐉⊤‖F2L(\mathbf{Z}):=\frac{1}{4}\left\|\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}^{\top}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{\top}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} with gradient ∇L​(𝐙)=(𝐙𝐙⊤−𝐉𝐉⊤)​𝐙\nabla L(\mathbf{Z})=\left(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}^{\top}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{\top}\right)\mathbf{Z}, and show that L⁡(⋅)L(\cdot) satisfies RC(4/σk2​(𝐉),9​σ12​(𝐉),σk​(𝐉)/4)(4/\sigma_{k}^{2}(\mathbf{J}),9\sigma_{1}^{2}(\mathbf{J}),\sigma_{k}(\mathbf{J})/4). Moreover, they prove that there exists an orthogonal matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} the gradient ∇L​(⋅)\nabla L(\cdot) satisfies the following inequality:

⟨∇L​(𝐙),𝐙−𝐉𝐑⟩≥σk2​(𝐉)4​‖𝐙−𝐉𝐑‖F2+14​‖𝐙𝐙⊤−𝐉𝐉⊤‖F2+120​‖(𝐙−𝐉𝐑)​𝐙⊤‖F2,\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla L(\mathbf{Z}),\mathbf{Z}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{R}\right\rangle\geq\frac{\sigma_{k}^{2}(\mathbf{J})}{4}\left\|\mathbf{Z}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{R}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\left\|\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}^{\top}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{\top}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\frac{1}{20}\left\|\left(\mathbf{Z}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{R}\right)\mathbf{Z}^{\top}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}, (16)

for any matrix 𝐙\mathbf{Z} obeying ‖𝐙−𝐉𝐑‖≤σk​(𝐉)/4\left\|\mathbf{Z}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{R}\right\|\leq\sigma_{k}(\mathbf{J})/4.

To prove Theorem 5.1, we examine the optimization landscape of the function g⁡(𝐙):=g⁡(𝐁,𝐖)g(\mathbf{Z}):=g(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{W}) in the lifted space ℝ(d+T)×k\mathbb{R}^{(d+T)\times k}. Therefore, we introduce several key block matrix operators and definitions. Let Sym:ℝd×T→ℝ(d+T)×(d+T)\Sym:\mathbb{R}^{d\times T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{(d+T)\times(d+T)} be defined as

Sym(𝐌):=(𝟎d×d𝐌𝐌⊤𝟎T×T)\Sym(\mathbf{M}):=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{0}_{d\times d}&\mathbf{M}\\ \mathbf{M}^{\top}&\mathbf{0}_{T\times T}\end{pmatrix}

𝐌=(𝐌11𝐌12𝐌21𝐌22),with𝐌11∈ℝd×d,𝐌12∈ℝd×T,𝐌21∈ℝT×d,𝐌22∈ℝT×T.\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{M}_{11}&\mathbf{M}_{12}\\ \mathbf{M}_{21}&\mathbf{M}_{22}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\text{with}\quad\mathbf{M}_{11}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d},\quad\mathbf{M}_{12}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T},\quad\mathbf{M}_{21}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d},\quad\mathbf{M}_{22}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T}.

Our final piece of notation is a matrix-valued map which works over lifted matrices, which we call 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The map 𝒞:ℝd×T:→ℝd×T\mathcal{C}:\mathbb{R}^{d\times T}:\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d\times T} is defined as

A.2 Proof of Theorem 5.4

For learning the future task parameter 𝐰T+1∗\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{*}, we employ a stochastic gradient descent (SGD) procedure with a geometrically decaying step size schedule (Algorithm 2). The step size of our algorithm remains constant for the first K2′+hK_{2}^{\prime}+h iterations, where hh denotes the length of the middle phase and K2′:=⌊K2−h/log⁡(K2−h)⌋K_{2}^{\prime}:=\lfloor K_{2}-h/\log(K_{2}-h)\rfloor. Subsequently, the step size is halved every K2′K_{2}^{\prime} steps. Specifically, the step size schedule is defined as follows:

ητ={η,0≤τ≤K2′+h,η/2l,K2′+h<τ≤K2,l=⌊(τ−h)/K2′⌋,\displaystyle\eta_{\tau}=\begin{cases}\eta,\quad&0\leq\tau\leq K_{2}^{\prime}+h,\\ \eta/2^{l},\quad&K_{2}^{\prime}+h<\tau\leq K_{2},\,\,l=\left\lfloor(\tau-h)/K_{2}^{\prime}\right\rfloor,\end{cases}

The combination of warm-up and learning rate decay has become a prevalent technique in deep learning optimization (Goyal et al., 2017). Among decay strategies, geometric schedules have shown superior empirical efficiency compared to polynomial decay, as they effectively balance rapid learning in early stages with stable refinement in late stages (Ge et al., 2019). Building on these advantages, we design our step size schedule to include an initial constant phase followed by a geometric decay stage.

During the training phase for future task T+1T+1, Algorithm 2 performs online iterative updates using the gradient of the following empirical loss function:

L^​(𝐰T+1):=12​(𝐱T+1⊤​𝐁^​𝐰T+1−yT+1)2.\displaystyle\widehat{L}(\mathbf{w}_{T+1}):=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{x}_{T+1}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\mathbf{w}_{T+1}-y_{T+1}\right)^{2}. (36)

The loss considered in this section resembles that of a linear model. However, according to the expression in Eq. (36), this loss additionally contains an irreducible error between 𝐁^\widehat{\mathbf{B}} and 𝐁∗\mathbf{B}^{*}. Consequently, compared with the typical dynamic of SGD with decaying step size in ordinary linear models (Wu et al., 2022), the dynamic of Algorithm 2 includes a component generated by additive noise that further involves stochastic noise correlated with the covariate vector 𝐱T+1\mathbf{x}_{T+1}. We resolve this correlation challenge by employing a recursive analysis technique. Moreover, in contrast to existing theoretical studies on transfer learning, our analysis requires only weaker moment assumptions.

According to the assumption for the output data yT+1y_{T+1}, we have

yT+1=𝐱T+1⊤​𝐁∗​𝐰T+1∗+zT+1=𝐱T+1⊤​𝐅𝐏𝐰T+1∗+zT+1,y_{T+1}=\mathbf{x}_{T+1}^{\top}\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{*}+z_{T+1}=\mathbf{x}_{T+1}^{\top}\mathbf{F}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{w}_{T+1}^{*}+z_{T+1},

Notations. Before proceeding with the subsequent analysis, we summarize the linear operators acting on symmetric matrices that will be employed in the proof.

ℐ\displaystyle\mathcal{I} :=𝐈k⊗𝐈k,ℋ:=𝔼⁡[(𝐱^T+1​𝐱^T+1⊤)⊗(𝐱^T+1​𝐱^T+1⊤)],ℋ~:=𝐁^⊤​𝐇​𝐁^⊗𝐁^⊤​𝐇​𝐁^,\displaystyle:=\mathbf{I}_{k}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{k},\quad\mathcal{H}:=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{T+1}\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{T+1}^{\top}\right)\otimes\left(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{T+1}\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{T+1}^{\top}\right)\right],\quad\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}:=\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\otimes\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\widehat{\mathbf{B}},

(ℐ−ητ​𝒢(τ))∘𝐌=𝔼⁡[(𝐈k−ητ​𝐱^T+1​𝐱^T+1⊤)​𝐌​(𝐈−ητ​𝐱^T+1​𝐱^T+1⊤)],\displaystyle\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\qquad\left(\mathcal{I}-\eta_{\tau}\mathcal{G}^{(\tau)}\right)\circ\mathbf{M}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\mathbf{I}_{k}-\eta_{\tau}\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{T+1}\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{T+1}^{\top}\right)\mathbf{M}\left(\mathbf{I}-\eta_{\tau}\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{T+1}\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{T+1}^{\top}\right)\right],

To establish the convergence result for the future task, we begin by analyzing the recursive properties of the matrices 𝐕(τ)\mathbf{V}^{(\tau)} and 𝐁(τ)\mathbf{B}^{(\tau)}, defined as follows:

A.2.3 Proof of Theorem 5.4

Notice that 𝐁^\widehat{\mathbf{B}} satisfies the condition of Theorem A.8 by utilizing Theorem 5.1 directly. Then the proof is completed by combining Eq. (41) with Theorem A.8 and Lemma A.9, and the estimation for ‖𝐁^​𝐑−𝐅‖F2\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{F}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} established in Theorem 5.1.

We further consider sequential curriculum learning, where parameters are learned sequentially across task groups. Curriculum learning manifests the principle of “starting small” (Wang et al., 2021), in which a model is initially trained on easier subsets of data before being gradually exposed to more difficult examples. This approach has demonstrated substantial improvements in training efficiency (Bengio et al., 2009; Hacohen and Weinshall, 2019; Narvekar et al., 2020). In our MTL setup, a curriculum consists of multiple tasks. By analogy, a course (e.g., advanced mathematics) contains multiple chapters, each can be treated as a task. We formulate task with lower additive noise variance as the “easier” curriculum, while task with higher additive noise variance constitutes the “harder” curriculum. Consider DD curricula categories, where the variance (σ(j))2​(j∈[D])\left(\sigma^{(j)}\right)^{2}(j\in[D]) of the additive noise is monotonically increasing, and the number of tasks in each category satisfies Tj≥dT_{j}\geq d. Our result (Corollary A.11) establishes that the curriculum strategy achieves a estimation error of 𝒪~​(k⁡(∑j=1D(σ(j))2​Tj)N⁡(∑j=1DTj))\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{k(\sum_{j=1}^{D}\left(\sigma^{(j)}\right)^{2}T_{j})}{N(\sum_{j=1}^{D}T_{j})}\right), which is substantially lower than the rate of 𝒪~​((σ(D))2​kN)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\left(\sigma^{(D)}\right)^{2}k}{N}\right) obtained by using all data indiscriminately when the noise variances are widely dispersed. As a result, we provide theoretical justification for curriculum learning in the context Linear MTL.

A.3 Curriculum Learning

The original concept of curriculum learning was formally introduced by Bengio et al. (2009), with its core principle being to ”train by progressing from simpler to more complex data.” This idea has since been expanded to a wide range of applications, including computer vision (CV) (Guo et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2014), natural language processing (NLP) (Platanios et al., 2019; Tay et al., 2019), and various reinforcement learning (RL) tasks (Florensa et al., 2017; Narvekar et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2018). Theoretically, Weinshall et al. (2018) defined the difficulty of a training sample (or curriculum) as its empirical loss relative to the optimal classifier. They demonstrated that, in the context of linear regression, curriculum learning can potentially lead to significantly accelerated learning.

In this section, we consider scenarios where task noise variances diverge. We partition the tasks into D D groups based on their noise levels and consider learning each group sequentially. This resembles curriculum learning, where tasks with lower variance are treated as an “easier” curriculum. For simplicity, we assume the number of tasks is large. Specifically, we study under the following assumption:

Assumption A.10.

For each task t∈[Tj]t\in[T_{j}] in curriculum level jj, the response yt,j∈ℝy_{t,j}\in\mathbb{R} givens the covariate 𝐱t,j∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{t,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is generated as follows:

yt,j=⟨𝐱t,j,𝐁∗​𝐰t,j∗⟩+zt,j,zt,j∼𝒩⁡(0,(σ(j))2).\displaystyle y_{t,j}=\left\langle\mathbf{x}_{t,j},\mathbf{B}^{*}\mathbf{w}_{t,j}^{*}\right\rangle+z_{t,j},\qquad z_{t,j}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,(\sigma^{(j)})^{2}\right).

Moreover, σ(1)≤σ(2)≤⋯≤σ(D)\sigma^{(1)}\leq\sigma^{(2)}\leq\cdots\leq\sigma^{(D)}.

For each curriculum level j∈[D]j\in[D], the number of tasks TjT_{j} satisfies Tj≥dT_{j}\geq d.

We study the multi-task data {(𝐱t,j,yt,j)}t=1Tj\{(\mathbf{x}_{t,j},y_{t,j})\}_{t=1}^{T_{j}} for j∈[D]j\in[D], generated under the Data Assumption introduced in Section 3. The noise levels in the data increase monotonically with the task index jj. This progression in noise creates a sequence of curriculum with ascending difficulty. Suppose the number of tasks exceeds the data dimension in each curriculum (Tj≥dT_{j}\geq d for all j∈[D]j\in[D]), the following Corollary A.11 specializes Theorem 5.1 to the setting of a DD-level curriculum. It provides a theoretical guarantee for the convergence of Algorithm 1 in curriculum learning, revealing a concrete benefit of a curriculum-like training approach for MTL.

‖𝐑t‖2=1N​maxu∈ℝT​⟨𝐯t∗,𝐮⟩2‖𝐮‖2​‖𝐗t​𝐳t‖2=1N​𝐳t⊤​𝐗t⊤​𝐗t​𝐳t⋅maxu∈ℝT⁡⟨𝐯t∗,𝐮⟩2‖𝐮‖2.\left\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\right\|^{2}=\frac{1}{N}\max_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{T}}\frac{\left\langle\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*},\mathbf{u}\right\rangle^{2}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}}\left\|\mathbf{X}_{t}\mathbf{z}_{t}\right\|^{2}=\frac{1}{N}\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\mathbf{z}_{t}\cdot\max_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{T}}\frac{\left\langle\mathbf{v}_{t}^{*},\mathbf{u}\right\rangle^{2}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}}.

Based on Hanson-Wright inequality, each 𝐑t\mathbf{R}_{t} has the following ℓ2\ell_{2} norm upper bound

‖𝐑t‖2≲σ2Ntr(𝐗t⊤𝐗t)+σ2​log⁡(δ~−1)N‖𝐗t⊤𝐗t‖+σ2​log12⁡(δ~−1)N‖𝐗t⊤𝐗t‖F,\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\right\|^{2}\lesssim\frac{\sigma^{2}}{N}\tr\left(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\right)+\frac{\sigma^{2}\log(\widetilde{\delta}^{-1})}{N}\left\|\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\right\|+\frac{\sigma^{2}\log^{\frac{1}{2}}(\widetilde{\delta}^{-1})}{N}\left\|\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}},

with probability at least 1−δ~1-\widetilde{\delta}. Since ‖𝐗t⊤​𝐗t‖F≤tr(𝐗t⊤​𝐗t)\left\|\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}\leq\tr\left(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\right), we define

L:=\displaystyle L:= [(1+δ)​(1+2​log⁡(δ~−1))​d]12\displaystyle\left[(1+\delta)\left(1+2\log\left(\widetilde{\delta}^{-1}\right)\right)d\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}
≥\displaystyle\geq [(1+log12⁡(δ~−1))Ntr(𝐗t⊤𝐗t)+log⁡(δ~−1)N‖𝐗t⊤𝐗t‖]12≥σ−1‖𝐑t‖.\displaystyle\left[\frac{\left(1+\log^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\widetilde{\delta}^{-1}\right)\right)}{N}\tr\left(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\right)+\frac{\log(\widetilde{\delta}^{-1})}{N}\left\|\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\right\|\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}\geq\sigma^{-1}\left\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\right\|.

According to the matrix bernstein (Theorem 7.3.1 in Tropp and others (2015)), we have

‖𝐘‖≲σ⁡[(𝐕𝐚𝐫)12+L]​log⁡(δ~−1)​log⁡(d𝐕),\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{Y}\right\|\lesssim\sigma\left[\left(\Var\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}+L\right]\log\left(\widetilde{\delta}^{-1}\right)\log\left(d_{\mathbf{V}}\right),

with probability at least 1−δ~1-\widetilde{\delta}, where 𝐕𝐚𝐫:=(𝟏+δ)​max​{𝐝,𝐓}≥σ−𝟐​max​{‖𝐕𝟏‖,‖𝐕𝟐‖}\Var:=(1+\delta)\max\left\{d,T\right\}\geq\sigma^{-2}\max\left\{\left\|\mathbf{V}_{1}\right\|,\left\|\mathbf{V}_{2}\right\|\right\}. ∎

Lemma B.2.

For diagonal positive definite matrix 𝚺∗∈ℝk×k\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k} and matrices 𝐔,𝐕∈ℝk×k\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}, suppose max⁡{‖𝐔‖,‖𝐕‖}≤C1​σmax12​(𝚺∗)\max\left\{\left\|\mathbf{U}\right\|,\left\|\mathbf{V}\right\|\right\}\leq C_{1}\sigma_{\max}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*}), ‖𝐔𝐕⊤−𝚺∗‖≤ϵ0\left\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}-\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*}\right\|\leq\epsilon_{0} and ‖𝐔−𝐕‖≤ϵ1\left\|\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{V}\right\|\leq\epsilon_{1}. Proof.

Since ‖𝐔𝐕⊤−𝚺∗‖≤ϵ0\left\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}-\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*}\right\|\leq\epsilon_{0} and ‖𝐔−𝐕‖≤ϵ1\left\|\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{V}\right\|\leq\epsilon_{1}, we have

‖(𝚺∗−12​𝐔)​(𝚺∗−12​𝐕)⊤−𝐈k‖≤σmin−1​(𝚺∗)​ϵ0 and ‖𝚺∗−12​𝐔−𝚺∗−12​𝐕‖≤σmin−12​(𝚺∗)​ϵ1.\displaystyle\left\|\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{U}\right)\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{V}\right)^{\top}-\mathbf{I}_{k}\right\|\leq\sigma_{\min}^{-1}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*})\epsilon_{0}\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\|\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{V}\right\|\leq\sigma_{\min}^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*})\epsilon_{1}. ‖𝐔∗​𝐔∗⊤−𝐈k‖≤\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{U}_{*}\mathbf{U}_{*}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}_{k}\right\|\leq ‖𝐔∗​𝐔∗⊤−𝐔∗​𝐕∗⊤‖+‖𝐔∗​𝐕∗⊤−𝐈k‖\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{U}_{*}\mathbf{U}_{*}^{\top}-\mathbf{U}_{*}\mathbf{V}_{*}^{\top}\right\|+\left\|\mathbf{U}_{*}\mathbf{V}_{*}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}_{k}\right\| (67)
≤\displaystyle\leq σmin−12​(𝚺∗)​‖𝐔∗‖​ϵ1+σmin−1​(𝚺∗)​ϵ0≤κ⁡(𝚺∗)​ϵ1+σmin−1​(𝚺∗)​ϵ0.\displaystyle\sigma_{\min}^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*})\left\|\mathbf{U}_{*}\right\|\epsilon_{1}+\sigma_{\min}^{-1}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*})\epsilon_{0}\leq\kappa(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*})\epsilon_{1}+\sigma_{\min}^{-1}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{*})\epsilon_{0}.

Consider the singular value decomposition (SVD) of 𝐔∗\mathbf{U}_{*} and 𝐕∗\mathbf{V}_{*}:

𝐔∗=𝐏𝐔∗​𝚺𝐔∗​𝐐𝐔∗⊤ and 𝐕∗=𝐏𝐕∗​𝚺𝐕∗​𝐐𝐕∗⊤,\mathbf{U}_{*}=\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}_{*}}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{U}_{*}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{U}_{*}}^{\top}\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathbf{V}_{*}=\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}_{*}}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{V}_{*}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{V}_{*}}^{\top},

where (a) follows from combining Eq.(66) and Eqs. (68)-(69). Utilizing Eqs. (69)-(70), we obtain
